## The premise

Field Notes is a data journal with one rule: every piece starts from real data, runs on
code you can see, and ends somewhere I didn't fully expect. The *method* is the throughline —
downloading the raw numbers, analyzing them honestly, and drawing conclusions that are, per
the tagline, questionable by design. The *topics* are whatever I'm currently obsessed with.

Mostly that's **credit markets, economics, and AI** — with the occasional detour into
whatever else the data makes interesting. If that range looks scattered, it isn't: it's one
person following curiosity with a consistent standard. You're subscribing to the analysis,
not the subject.

## Who's writing this

I'm a credit analyst by day, which means I spend a lot of time with data that most people
are content to see summarized in someone else's chart with a footnote reading *"Source:
Federal Reserve."* I'm more interested in where those numbers come from, and what the raw
data actually shows when you look at it directly.

## How to read it

- **Real data, shown.** Every chart traces back to a public source, cited.
- **Real code, shared.** The analysis is reproducible — the code folds open on the page.
- **Conclusions, questionable.** This is descriptive, not advice. Here's what the data shows,
  here's the method, here's where it's incomplete.

Topics are tagged — **Credit**, **Economics**, **AI**, and more as they come up — so you can
follow a thread or take the whole grab-bag.

See [Data & methods](data-sources.qmd) for how the data gets from source to page.
